claim: From a cohort of 167 infertile patients suffering from multiple morphological abnormalities of the flagellum (MMAF), pathogenic bi-allelic mutations were identified in the CCDC146 gene.
source: From a cohort of 167 infertile patients suffering from multiple morphological abnormalities of the flagellum (MMAF), pathogenic bi-allelic mutations were identified in the CCDC146 gene.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-exome sequencing data from the patient cohort, identifying specific mutations in CCDC146.

claim: In somatic cells, CCDC146 is located at the centrosome and at multiple microtubule-related organelles during mitotic division.
source: In somatic cells, CCDC146 is located at the centrosome and at multiple microtubule-related organelles during mitotic division, suggesting that it is a microtubule-associated protein (MAP).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence experiments showing CCDC146 localization in somatic cells.

claim: CCDC146 is a microtubule-associated protein (MAP).
source: In somatic cells, CCDC146 is located at the centrosome and at multiple microtubule-related organelles during mitotic division, suggesting that it is a microtubule-associated protein (MAP).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed localization patterns of CCDC146 at microtubule-related structures.

claim: A Ccdc146 knock-out (KO) mouse line was created to decipher the molecular pathogenesis of infertility associated with CCDC146 mutations.
source: To decipher the molecular pathogenesis of infertility associated with CCDC146 mutations, a Ccdc146 knock-out (KO) mouse line was created.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the experimental approach using CRISPR/Cas9 technology to generate the mouse model.

claim: KO male mice were infertile.
source: KO male mice were infertile, and sperm exhibited a phenotype identical to CCDC146 mutated patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by fertility testing data showing no offspring from KO males.

claim: Sperm from KO male mice exhibited a phenotype identical to CCDC146 mutated patients.
source: KO male mice were infertile, and sperm exhibited a phenotype identical to CCDC146 mutated patients.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological analysis of sperm from both KO mice and human patients.

claim: CCDC146 expression starts during late spermiogenesis.
source: CCDC146 expression starts during late spermiogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data showing Ccdc146 expression during the first wave of spermatogenesis.

claim: In the spermatozoon, CCDC146 is conserved but is not localized to centrioles, unlike in somatic cells.
source: In the spermatozoon, the protein is conserved but is not localized to centrioles, unlike in somatic cells, rather it is present in the axoneme at the level of microtubule doublets.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and Western blot data showing CCDC146 localization in sperm.

claim: In the spermatozoon, CCDC146 is present in the axoneme at the level of microtubule doublets.
source: In the spermatozoon, the protein is conserved but is not localized to centrioles, unlike in somatic cells, rather it is present in the axoneme at the level of microtubule doublets.
evidence: The claim is supported by expansion microscopy data showing CCDC146 association with microtubule doublets.

claim: CCDC146 may be a microtubule inner protein (MIP).
source: Expansion microscopy associated with the use of the detergent sarkosyl to solubilize microtubule doublets suggests that the protein may be a microtubule inner protein (MIP).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from sarkosyl solubilization experiments and expansion microscopy observations.

claim: The absence of CCDC146 impacted all microtubule-based organelles such as the manchette, the head–tail coupling apparatus (HTCA), and the axoneme.
source: At the subcellular level, the absence of CCDC146 impacted all microtubule-based organelles such as the manchette, the head–tail coupling apparatus (HTCA), and the axoneme.
evidence: The claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy and immunofluorescence data showing defects in these structures in KO mice.

claim: Infertility affects approximately 50 million couples worldwide.
source: Infertility is a major health concern, affecting approximately 50 million couples worldwide (Boivin et al., 2007), or 12.5% of women and 10% of men.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Boivin et al., 2007.

claim: Infertility affects 12.5% of women and 10% of men.
source: Infertility is a major health concern, affecting approximately 50 million couples worldwide (Boivin et al., 2007), or 12.5% of women and 10% of men.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Boivin et al., 2007.

claim: Infertility is defined by the World Health Organization (WHO) as the 'failure to achieve a pregnancy after 12 months or more of regular unprotected sexual intercourse'.
source: It is defined by the World Health Organization (WHO) as the "failure to achieve a pregnancy after 12 months or more of regular unprotected sexual intercourse".
evidence: The claim is based on the WHO definition of infertility, which is established scientific knowledge.

claim: There are now 5 million people born as a result of ART.
source: In almost all countries, infertile couples have access to assisted reproductive technology (ART) to try to conceive a baby, and there are now 5 million people born as a result of ART.
evidence: The claim is presented as a factual statement about the outcomes of ART, likely based on established data.

claim: Almost half of the couples seeking medical support for infertility fail to successfully conceive and bear a child by the end of their medical care.
source: Despite this success, almost half of the couples seeking medical support for infertility fail to successfully conceive and bear a child by the end of their medical care.
evidence: The claim is presented as a factual statement about ART outcomes, likely based on established data.

claim: The main reason for ART failures is that one member of the couple produces gametes that are unable to support fertilization and/or embryonic development.
source: The main reason for these failures is that one member of the couple produces gametes that are unable to support fertilization and/or embryonic development.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the understanding of reproductive biology and ART limitations.

claim: ART does not specifically treat or even try to elucidate the underlying causes of a couple's infertility, rather it tries to bypass the observed defects.
source: Indeed, ART does not specifically treat or even try to elucidate the underlying causes of a couple's infertility, rather it tries to bypass the observed defects.
evidence: The claim is based on the understanding of how ART works, which is established knowledge in reproductive medicine.

claim: More than 4000 genes are thought to be involved in sperm production.
source: Genetic defects play a major role in male infertility, with over 4000 genes thought to be involved in sperm production, of which more than 2000 are testis-enriched and almost exclusively involved in spermatogenesis (Uhlén et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Uhlén et al., 2016.

claim: More than 2000 genes involved in sperm production are testis-enriched and almost exclusively involved in spermatogenesis.
source: Genetic defects play a major role in male infertility, with over 4000 genes thought to be involved in sperm production, of which more than 2000 are testis-enriched and almost exclusively involved in spermatogenesis (Uhlén et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Uhlén et al., 2016.

claim: Today, more than 120 genes are associated with all types of male infertility.
source: Today, more than 120 genes are associated with all types of male infertility (Houston et al., 2021), including quantitative and qualitative sperm defects.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Houston et al., 2021.

claim: Around 50 genes have been identified as coding for proteins involved in MMAF syndrome.
source: Study of the MMAF phenotype in humans has allowed the identification of around 50 genes (Wang et al., 2022) coding for proteins involved in axonemal organization, present in the structures surrounding the axoneme – such as the outer dense fibers and the fibrous sheath – and involved in intra-flagellar transport (IFT).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2022.

claim: Only around half (10 of the 22 PCD-related genes identified so far) are effectively associated with male infertility.
source: However, this structural similarity does not necessarily imply a molecular similarity, and only around half (10 of the 22 PCD-related genes identified so far; Sironen et al., 2020) are effectively associated with male infertility.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sironen et al., 2020.

claim: Biallelic deleterious variants in 22 genes were identified in 83 subjects from a cohort of 167 MMAF patients.
source: We have recruited 167 patients with MMAF. Following WES, biallelic deleterious variants in 22 genes were identified in 83 subjects.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-exome sequencing data from the patient cohort.

claim: A molecular diagnosis is obtained in half of the patients (49.7%) with MMAF phenotype.
source: Despite this success, a molecular diagnosis is obtained in half of the patients (49.7%) with this sperm phenotype, suggesting that novel candidate genes remain to be identified.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis of the patient cohort data.

claim: Bi-allelic truncating mutations in CCDC146 were identified in two unrelated infertile patients displaying MMAF.
source: As such, we have identified bi-allelic truncating mutations in CCDC146 in two unrelated infertile patients displaying MMAF.
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-exome sequencing and Sanger sequencing data.

claim: CCDC146 is known to code for a centrosomal protein when heterologously expressed in HeLa cells.
source: CCDC146 is known to code for a centrosomal protein when heterologously expressed in HeLa cells (Firat-Karalar et al., 2014; Almeida et al., 2018), but minimal information is available on its distribution within the cell, or its function when naturally present.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Firat-Karalar et al., 2014 and Almeida et al., 2018.

claim: CCDC146 has never been associated with any human disease.
source: Moreover, this gene has never been associated with any human disease.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of prior reports linking CCDC146 to disease, which is established knowledge.

claim: The centrosome is the major microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) in animal cells.
source: The centrosome is the major microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) in animal cells, and as such regulates the microtubule organization within the cell.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of cell biology.

claim: 3% (579 proteins) of all known human proteins have been experimentally detected in the centrosome.
source: The importance of this organelle is highlighted by the fact that 3% (579 proteins) of all known human proteins have been experimentally detected in the centrosome (https://www.proteinatlas.org/humanproteome/subcellular/centrosome).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the Human Protein Atlas database.

claim: In round spermatids, the centriole pair docks to the cell membrane, whereas the distal centriole serves as the basal body initiating assembly of the axoneme.
source: In round spermatids, the centriole pair docks to the cell membrane, whereas the distal centriole serves as the basal body initiating assembly of the axoneme.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of spermatogenesis.

claim: The proximal centriole tightly attaches to the sperm nucleus and gradually develops the head-to-tail coupling apparatus (HTCA), linking the sperm head to the flagellum.
source: The proximal centriole then tightly attaches to the sperm nucleus and gradually develops the head-to-tail coupling apparatus (HTCA), linking the sperm head to the flagellum (Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2020.

claim: In human and bovine sperm, the proximal centriole is retained and the distal centriole is remodeled to produce an 'atypical' centriole.
source: In human and bovine sperm, the proximal centriole is retained and the distal centriole is remodeled to produce an 'atypical' centriole Fishman et al., 2018 in contrast, in rodents, both centrioles are degenerated during epididymal maturation (Manandhar et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fishman et al., 2018 and Manandhar et al., 1998.

claim: In rodents, both centrioles are degenerated during epididymal maturation.
source: In human and bovine sperm, the proximal centriole is retained and the distal centriole is remodeled to produce an 'atypical' centriole Fishman et al., 2018 in contrast, in rodents, both centrioles are degenerated during epididymal maturation (Manandhar et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Manandhar et al., 1998.

claim: Very few centrosomal proteins have been linked to MMAF in humans – so far only CEP135, CEP148, or DZIP1.
source: Despite the number of proteins making up the centrosome, and its importance in sperm differentiation and flagellum formation, very few centrosomal proteins have been linked to MMAF in humans – so far only CEP135 (Sha et al., 2017), CEP148 (Zhang et al., 2022), or DZIP1 (Lv et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sha et al., 2017, Zhang et al., 2022, and Lv et al., 2020.

claim: Some major axonemal proteins with an accessory location in the centrosome, such as CFAP58 and ODF2, have been reported to be involved in MMAF syndrome.
source: Moreover, some major axonemal proteins with an accessory location in the centrosome, such as CFAP58 (Sha et al., 2021) and ODF2 (Zhu et al., 2022; Nakagawa et al., 2001), have also been reported to be involved in MMAF syndrome.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sha et al., 2021, Zhu et al., 2022, and Nakagawa et al., 2001.

claim: Other centrosomal proteins lead to MMAF in mice; these include CEP131 and CCDC42.
source: Other centrosomal proteins lead to MMAF in mice; these include CEP131 (Hall et al., 2013) and CCDC42 (Pasek et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hall et al., 2013 and Pasek et al., 2016.

claim: The first identified mutation in CCDC146 is located in exon 9 and corresponds to c.1084C>T.
source: The first identified mutation is located in exon 9 and corresponds to c.1084C>T, the second is located in exon 15 and corresponds to c.2112Del (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-exome sequencing and Sanger sequencing data.

claim: The second identified mutation in CCDC146 is located in exon 15 and corresponds to c.2112Del.
source: The first identified mutation is located in exon 9 and corresponds to c.1084C>T, the second is located in exon 15 and corresponds to c.2112Del (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-exome sequencing and Sanger sequencing data.

claim: The c.1084C>T variant is a nonsense mutation.
source: The c.1084C>T variant is a nonsense mutation, whereas the single-nucleotide deletion c.2112Del is predicted to induce a translational frameshift.
evidence: The claim is based on the analysis of the mutation type.

claim: The single-nucleotide deletion c.2112Del is predicted to induce a translational frameshift.
source: The c.1084C>T variant is a nonsense mutation, whereas the single-nucleotide deletion c.2112Del is predicted to induce a translational frameshift.
evidence: The claim is based on the analysis of the mutation type.

claim: Both mutations in CCDC146 were predicted to produce premature stop codons: p.(Arg362Ter) and p.(Arg704serfsTer7).
source: Both mutations were predicted to produce premature stop codons: p.(Arg362Ter) and p.(Arg704serfsTer7), respectively, leading either to the complete absence of the protein or to the production of a truncated and non-functional protein.
evidence: The claim is based on the analysis of the mutations and their predicted effects on protein translation.

claim: These variants are annotated with a high impact on the protein structure (MoBiDiC prioritization algorithm [MPA] score = 10).
source: These variants are annotated with a high impact on the protein structure (MoBiDiC prioritization algorithm [MPA] score = 10) (Yauy et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by the MPA score and a citation to Yauy et al., 2018.

claim: The two mutations in CCDC146 are most likely deleterious.
source: The two mutations are therefore most likely deleterious.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the predicted effects of the mutations on protein structure and function.

claim: Both variants in CCDC146 were absent in the control cohort.
source: Both variants were absent in our control cohort and their minor allele frequencies (MAF), according to the gnomAD v3 database, were 6.984 × 10–5 and 6.5 × 10–06, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by the analysis of the control cohort and gnomAD database.

claim: The minor allele frequencies (MAF) of the two CCDC146 variants, according to the gnomAD v3 database, were 6.984 × 10–5 and 6.5 × 10–06, respectively.
source: Both variants were absent in our control cohort and their minor allele frequencies (MAF), according to the gnomAD v3 database, were 6.984 × 10–5 and 6.5 × 10–06, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the gnomAD v3 database.

claim: The Ccdc146 KO mice were viable without apparent defects.
source: The Ccdc146 KO mice were viable without apparent defects.
evidence: The claim is supported by the observation of the KO mice.

claim: WT or heterozygous animals and KO females were fertile.
source: WT or heterozygous animals and KO females were fertile, whereas KO males were completely infertile (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fertility testing data.

claim: Infertility in KO males is associated with a 90% decrease in epididymal sperm concentration (from ~30 to ~3 million).
source: This infertility is associated with a 90% decrease in epididymal sperm concentration (from ~30 to ~3 million) (Figure 2B) and a significant decrease of testicle weight relative to whole body weight (Figure 2C), suggesting a germ cell rarefaction in the seminiferous epithelia due to high apoptosis level.
evidence: The claim is supported by sperm concentration measurements.

claim: Infertility in KO males is associated with a significant decrease of testicle weight relative to whole body weight.
source: This infertility is associated with a 90% decrease in epididymal sperm concentration (from ~30 to ~3 million) (Figure 2B) and a significant decrease of testicle weight relative to whole body weight (Figure 2C), suggesting a germ cell rarefaction in the seminiferous epithelia due to high apoptosis level.
evidence: The claim is supported by testis weight measurements.

claim: A study of spermatogenic cell viability by TUNEL assay confirmed a significant increase in the number of fluorescent cells in Ccdc146 KO animals.
source: A study of spermatogenic cell viability by TUNEL assay confirmed this hypothesis, with a significant increase in the number of fluorescent cells in Ccdc146 KO animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL assay data.

claim: Sperm morphology in Ccdc146 KO mice was strongly altered, with a typical MMAF phenotype and marked defects in head morphology.
source: Closer examination revealed sperm morphology to be strongly altered, with a typical MMAF phenotype and marked defects in head morphology (Figure 2D) indicative of significantly impaired spermiogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological analysis of sperm.

claim: The percentage of abnormal form, flagellum and head anomalies in Ccdc146 KO sperm is 100%.
source: The percentage of abnormal form, flagellum and head anomalies is 100% (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological analysis of sperm.

claim: An almost complete absence of motility was observed in Ccdc146 KO sperm.
source: Moreover, an almost complete absence of motility was observed (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by sperm motility analysis.

claim: On sections of spermatogenic tubules, structural and shape defects were present from the elongating spermatid stage in Ccdc146 KO mice.
source: Comparative histological studies (Figure 3) showed that on sections of spermatogenic tubules, structural and shape defects were present from the elongating spermatid stage in Ccdc146 KO mice, with almost complete disappearance of the flagella in the lumen and very long spermatid nuclei (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis.

claim: Transverse sections of the epididymal tubules from KO males contained almost no spermatozoa, and the tubules were filled with an acellular substance.
source: At the epididymal level, transverse sections of the epididymal tubules from KO males contained almost no spermatozoa, and the tubules were filled with an acellular substance (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological analysis.

claim: In HEK-293T cells, CCDC146 colocalized with centrioles.
source: In HEK-293T cells, using an antibody recognizing centrin (anti-centrin Ab) as a centriole marker and the anti-CCDC146 Ab, CCDC146 was shown to colocalize with centrioles.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: The CCDC146 signal was not strictly localized to centrioles, as peri-centriolar labeling was clearly visible.
source: However, the signal was not strictly localized to centrioles, as peri-centriolar labeling was clearly visible (Figure 4A1d, overlay).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: CCDC146 was observed on the basal body of primary cilia in cells cultured under serum-deprived conditions.
source: Finally, the presence of CCDC146 was assessed at the basal body of primary cilia in cells cultured under serum-deprived conditions (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: Both centrioles pairs were stained by CCDC146 Ab in cells blocked in the G2 phase.
source: Both centrioles pairs were stained by CCDC146 Ab in cells blocked in the G2 phase (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data on synchronized cells.

claim: In non-synchronized cells, the mitotic spindle was labeled at its base and at its ends by CCDC146.
source: In non-synchronized cells, the mitotic spindle was labeled at its base and at its ends (Figure 5BC).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: The co-labeling of CCDC146 intensified in the midzone during chromatid separation.
source: The co-labeling intensified in the midzone during chromatid separation (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: The separation structure between the two cells, the midbody, was strongly stained by CCDC146.
source: Finally, the separation structure between the two cells, the midbody, was also strongly stained (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: Identical labeling profiles of CCDC146 were observed in freshly prepared human foreskin fibroblasts (HFF cells).
source: Identical labeling profiles were observed in freshly prepared human foreskin fibroblasts (HFF cells) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data on primary cells.

claim: The protein CCDC146 was retained in epididymal sperm, where one band was observed around 120 kDa.
source: Interestingly, the protein was retained in epididymal sperm, where one band was observed around 120 kDa (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data.

claim: The theoretical MW of the HA-tagged CCDC146 protein is around 116.2 kDa (115.1 + 1.1).
source: The theoretical MW of the tagged protein is around 116.2 kDa (115.1 + 1.1); the observed MW was slightly higher, suggesting that the protein migrates at a different weight or some post-translational modifications.
evidence: The claim is based on the calculation of the theoretical molecular weight of the protein.

claim: In the flagella fraction, the HA Ab revealed a band with an intensity similar to that of the whole sperm at around 120 kDa, whereas no staining was observed in head fraction.
source: In the flagella fraction, the HA Ab revealed a band with an intensity similar to that of the whole sperm at around 120 kDa, whereas no staining was observed in head fraction.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data on fractionated sperm.

claim: Extremely low Ccdc146 expression was detected at day 9, corresponding to testes containing spermatogonia and Sertoli cells only.
source: Extremely low Ccdc146 expression was detected at day 9, corresponding to testes containing spermatogonia and Sertoli cells only.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data during the first wave of spermatogenesis.

claim: Ccdc146 expression was observed from postnatal day 18 (formation of secondary spermatocytes).
source: Ccdc146 expression was observed from postnatal day 18 (formation of secondary spermatocytes), peaked at day 26 (formation of elongated spermatids), and subsequently decreased from day 35 (formation of spermatozoa), suggesting that Ccdc146 is particularly expressed in elongated spermatids during spermatogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data during the first wave of spermatogenesis.

claim: Ccdc146 expression peaked at day 26 (formation of elongated spermatids).
source: Ccdc146 expression was observed from postnatal day 18 (formation of secondary spermatocytes), peaked at day 26 (formation of elongated spermatids), and subsequently decreased from day 35 (formation of spermatozoa), suggesting that Ccdc146 is particularly expressed in elongated spermatids during spermatogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data during the first wave of spermatogenesis.

claim: Ccdc146 expression subsequently decreased from day 35 (formation of spermatozoa).
source: Ccdc146 expression was observed from postnatal day 18 (formation of secondary spermatocytes), peaked at day 26 (formation of elongated spermatids), and subsequently decreased from day 35 (formation of spermatozoa), suggesting that Ccdc146 is particularly expressed in elongated spermatids during spermatogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-PCR data during the first wave of spermatogenesis.

claim: A punctiform labeling was observed along the whole flagellum in HA-CCDC146 sperm.
source: In conventional IF, using an HA Tag Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated Antibody (anti-HA-AF488-C Ab), a punctiform labeling was observed along the whole flagellum (Figure 7A) on HA-CCDC146 only.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: A highly significant difference in the density of dots in the principal piece of WT and HA-CCDC146 sperm was found, with a p-value<0.0001.
source: We found a highly significant difference, with a p-value<0.0001, showing that the signal obtained on spermatozoa expressing the tagged protein is highly specific.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of immunofluorescence data.

claim: The mouse flagellum presented breaks that most likely resulted from the expansion procedure.
source: Unexpectedly, the mouse flagellum presented breaks that most likely resulted from the expansion procedure (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation of breaks in expansion microscopy.

claim: Strong HA labeling was observed at the level of breaks in the mouse flagellum, suggesting that CCDC146 epitopes are buried inside the axonemal structure and become accessible mostly on blunt or broken microtubule doublets.
source: Interestingly, strong HA labeling was observed at the level of these breaks, suggesting that CCDC146 epitopes are buried inside the axonemal structure and become accessible mostly on blunt or broken microtubule doublets.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation of strong labeling at breaks in expansion microscopy.

claim: No colocalization of the CCDC146 label with centrin was observed on human sperm centrioles.
source: No colocalization of the CCDC146 label with centrin was observed on human sperm centrioles (Figure 8A1d, A2d, and A3d), suggesting that the protein is not present in or around this structure.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: Two unexpected labeling events were observed in human sperm: sub-acrosomal labeling and labeling of the midpiece.
source: However, two unexpected labeling events were observed: sub-acrosomal labeling and labeling of the midpiece (Figure 8A1b, A2b, and A3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: Faint staining was observed along the whole length of the human sperm flagellum.
source: At the flagellum level, faint staining was observed along the whole length (Figure 8A4b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: U-ExM unveiled that the observed CCDC146 midpiece staining seems in fact associated with isolated structures, which could be mitochondria.
source: Moreover, U-ExM unveiled that the observed CCDC146 midpiece staining (Figure 8A) seems in fact associated with isolated structures, which we hypothesize could be mitochondria, now visible by expansion (Figure 8B1).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from expansion microscopy observations.

claim: Clear punctiform labeling was observed along the whole length of the principal piece of the human sperm flagellum.
source: In contrast, at the flagellum level, clear punctiform labeling was observed along the whole length of the principal piece (Figure 8B1 and B5), confirming that the protein is present in the sperm flagellum.
evidence: The claim is supported by expansion microscopy data.

claim: Labeling of CCDC146 was preferentially located on the right and left doublets of the axoneme.
source: Labeling was preferentially located on the right and left doublets (Figure 9D), indicating that CCDC146 associates more with microtubule doublets.
evidence: The claim is supported by expansion microscopy data and quantitative analysis.

claim: On some spermatozoa with frayed microtubule doublets, isolated doublets carried the punctiform labeling confirming the results of analyses on human spermatozoa.
source: Nevertheless, using U-ExM, on some spermatozoa with frayed microtubule doublets, that is, with the flagellum taking on the shape of a hair, we could find that isolated doublets carried the punctiform labeling confirming the results of analyses on human spermatozoa (Figure 9E).
evidence: The claim is supported by expansion microscopy data on mouse sperm.

claim: CCDC146 is an axonemal protein, probably associated with microtubule doublets.
source: Taken together, these results from mouse and human sperm demonstrate that CCDC146 is an axonemal protein, probably associated with microtubule doublets.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from multiple lines of evidence including expansion microscopy and biochemical data.

claim: The protein CCDC146 was effectively solubilized by sarkosyl, leading to the appearance of bands at around 120 kDa on an SDS-PAGE gel following migration of extracts from sperm treated with 0.2 and 0.4% sarkosyl concentrations.
source: The protein was effectively solubilized, leading to the appearance of bands at around 120 kDa on an SDS-PAGE gel following migration of extracts from sperm treated with 0.2 and 0.4% sarkosyl concentrations.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data on sarkosyl-treated sperm.

claim: A second band around 90 kDa was also immunodecorated by anti-HA antibody in the sarkosyl treated sample, which may correspond to proteolytic fragment of CCDC146.
source: Interestingly, a second band around 90 kDa was also immunodecorated by anti-HA antibody in the sarkosyl treated sample, a band not present in the protein extracts from WT males. This band may correspond to proteolytic fragment of CCDC146, the solubilization of microtubules by sarkosyl may have made CCDC146 more accessible to endogenous proteases.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from Western blot data and speculation about the nature of the band.

claim: The other detergents and buffers tested – RIPA, CHAPS, or Tris-HCl – barely solubilized CCDC146 or led to no solubilization.
source: The other detergents and buffers tested – RIPA, CHAPS, or Tris-HCl – barely solubilized CCDC146 or led to no solubilization (Figure 10B, Figure 10—source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data on sperm treated with different detergents.

claim: CCDC146 labeling in the principal piece was significantly increased in the presence of sarkosyl.
source: CCDC146 labeling in the principal piece was significantly increased in the presence of sarkosyl (Figure 10C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data on sarkosyl-treated sperm.

claim: In Ccdc146 KO sperm, there was a great variability in the morphological defects of the connecting piece, some were almost intact, whereas others were severely damaged.
source: In Ccdc146 KO sperm, there was a great variability in the morphological defects of the connecting piece, some were almost intact (Figure 11A2), whereas others were severely damaged (Figure 11A3 and A4).
evidence: The claim is supported by scanning electron microscopy data.

claim: In WT testicular sperm, the centrioles, identified by anti-tubulin Ab, are very close to each other and adjacent to the nucleus.
source: In WT testicular sperm, IF experiments show that the centrioles, identified by anti-tubulin Ab, are very close to each other and adjacent to the nucleus (Figure 11B1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: For Ccdc146 KO males, although some sperm cells presented centrioles with almost normal localization, centriole separation was visible in numerous spermatozoa.
source: For Ccdc146 KO males, although some sperm cells presented centrioles with almost normal localization (Figure 11B2), centriole separation was visible in numerous spermatozoa (Figure 11B3 and B4), with the structures located far away from the connecting piece (Figure 11B5) or duplicated (Figure 11B6).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data.

claim: The overall structure of the HTCA under construction in spermatids, observed by TEM, was conserved in Ccdc146 KO spermatids, with the presence of both centrioles, containing nine triplets of microtubules, as well as accessory cytoskeletal structures, including the capitulum and the segmented columns.
